1.goal: To open the lesson on what it is: the message that arrives before the meeting, and what happens once he has understood it.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is accepted here.
run: Ask about the last message in English he read all the way through and did not answer straight away. One answer, then move.
This is his first lesson. Say, in one sentence, that today's production is recorded and is the zero mark — he asked for evidence of progress in as many words.
1.expected: One concrete message, most likely from this week.
1.support: If nothing comes, ask about the last one he answered late rather than the last one he read.
1.challenge: Ask what he did instead of answering, and how long it took.
1.monitoring: Whether the delay he describes is about understanding or about producing the answer. Today is the second.
1.evidence: The example he gives — and that he heard, out loud, that today is the zero mark.
1.transition: Move on when he has given one concrete example.

2.goal: To establish who wrote, what they want, and what is at stake.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the card on screen together.
run: Give him time to read the card.
Confirm two things out loud: they do not know his company yet, and the list closes on Thursday.
2.expected: Immediate recognition. This is his inbox.
2.support: If the stakes stay abstract, ask what happens on Friday if the answer does not arrive.
2.challenge: Ask what he would want to know about Diane before answering.
2.monitoring: He will want to discuss the deal. Let it happen ONCE, here, and then hold the route — deal talk is how his previous lessons turned into lessons he was running.
2.evidence: Whether he can state what she wants in one sentence.
2.transition: Move on when he says, in one sentence, what this person wants from him.

3.goal: To activate what he already knows about this kind of message, BEFORE reading it.
3.interaction: T–S, three open questions. Portuguese accepted, and given back in English.
run: Read the three questions WITH him, out loud, and ask for a guess on each.
Do not correct: these are hypotheses.
If he answers in Portuguese, take the idea and say it back in English for him to repeat. Do not stop the idea to fix the language.
exact: Giving his idea back in English: “So you are saying they are measuring how fast you answer. In English: they are measuring your response time. Say it back to me.”
3.expected: He has repertoire to spare — he has sat on both sides of this table in Portuguese. Let him talk.
3.support: If a guess comes in one word, ask “why that one?” once.
3.challenge: Ask which of the three he would bet on, and what he would do about it.
3.monitoring: Whether the English comes back when you offer it, or the idea stays in Portuguese.
3.evidence: The reasons he gives — they come back in the two minutes at stage 8.
3.transition: Move on when he has risked all three.

4.goal: One whole reading, no pen, only to answer the two questions on screen.
4.interaction: S reads alone for ninety seconds, then T–S on two questions.
run: Ninety seconds of silent reading.
Then the two questions, out loud. Do not ask for a translation of anything.
If it is too easy, do not add text: cut the time.
exact: If he starts translating sentence by sentence: “In one sentence — what does she want?”
4.expected: He reads well. The three things asked for, even out of order.
4.support: If the reading turns into translation, stop and ask for the one-sentence version.
4.challenge: Ask which of the three requests he would answer first, and why that one.
4.monitoring: This is where the lesson can turn into translation. Watch for it in the first thirty seconds.
4.evidence: How he reads under no time pressure — the first reading sample of the cycle.
4.transition: Move on when he says the three things asked for, even out of order.

5.goal: To separate what was ASKED from what was merely implied — and from what is not there at all.
5.interaction: S classifies alone; you check and discuss only the misses.
run: He classifies, you check. Discuss only the ones he gets wrong.
5.expected: Six items sorted, with “how much they would pay” recognized as not in the email at all.
5.support: If an item resists, ask him to point at the line in the email that says it.
5.challenge: Ask what Diane would have written if she HAD asked about price.
5.monitoring: The item that decides: “how much they would pay” is NOT in the email. If he marks it as asked, he is reading what he would like to read — and it is worth naming, without softening. And “that they are talking to other companies” is implication (the word shortlist), not statement: it is the most useful reading in the whole email.
5.evidence: Whether he separates implication from statement without help.
5.transition: Move on when the six are checked.

6.goal: For HIM to formulate the difference between repeating and saying it back. Do not hand him the rule.
6.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S until he words it himself.
run: The four lines on screen. He marks the ones that say something back.
Then ask what the two he marked have in common.
Do not correct the language here. The object is the distinction.
exact: What do the two you marked have in common?
6.expected: The answer you want, from him and not from you: saying it back uses FEWER words than the original and states what he understood; repeating uses the other person's words and adds nothing.
6.support: If the distinction will not come, read one of each out loud and ask which one tells her something she did not already know.
6.challenge: Ask him to turn one of the repetitions into a saying-back, on the spot.
6.monitoring: Whether he reaches the distinction himself. Handing it over saves two minutes and costs the stage.
6.evidence: His own wording of the difference, however rough. It is what stage 7 practices.
6.transition: Move on when he has worded the difference himself.

7.goal: The six expressions said out loud, with the content coming from you.
7.interaction: T gives the raw content; S gives it back with the expression. Six, fast.
run: You say the raw content in Portuguese or in simple English (“they want to know how much of the revenue is recurring”) and he gives it back using the expression on screen. Six times, fast.
Correction here is immediate and dry — this is the form stage. At stage 8 there is no correcting.
exact: If he translates your whole sentence: “Same idea, half the words.”
7.expected: Six openings, each carrying the content in fewer words than you used.
7.support: If he translates your sentence whole, ask for the same idea in HALF the words. A short sentence breaks the transfer from Portuguese faster than any explanation.
7.challenge: Give two pieces of content at once and ask for one sentence that carries both.
7.monitoring: Whether the sentence gets shorter than yours, or stays the same length.
7.evidence: How many of the six come out without the screen.
7.transition: Move on when the six have each come out at least once.

8.goal: The production of the lesson — two minutes to a partner who has not read the email.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are the partner; the turn is his.
run: CLOSE THE EMAIL BEFORE HE STARTS. With the text in sight he reads, and reading out loud is not what this lesson measures.
Two minutes. Interrupt ONCE, in the middle, with a question of substance, and let him find his way back on his own.
After you ask, WAIT. The turn is his, and his silence is work.
Do not correct during. Note it — including the third-person agreement, which is lesson 3's object and not today's — and hand it back at stage 9.
Record it. It is his first production sample in English, and the comparison base for the whole cycle.
exact: And when do they need it?
8.expected: Two minutes that say who wrote, what they want and by when, in fewer words than the email.
8.support: If he stalls after the interruption, repeat his last sentence back as a question and wait.
8.challenge: Ask a second question at the end — “and what do we say about the price?” — and take the answer inside the two minutes.
8.monitoring: Whether he says it back or recites the email, and whether the deadline survives.
8.evidence: The recording. It is the zero mark of the cycle, and he asked for it.
8.transition: Move on when he closes, or at two minutes, whichever comes first.

9.goal: To hand back what you noted and to ask for it again, in a third of the time.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the board together, then one retask.
run: Two things, no more — one that worked and one that did not come out. Straight, without softening: he asked for hard correction and reads softening as tolerance.
Then: same thing, forty-five seconds, and the partner is already late for something.
Do not add new content here. It is the same task under one changed constraint.
exact: Same thing, forty-five seconds — and your partner is already late for something.
9.expected: The same content with the background gone and the request kept.
9.support: If he cannot cut, ask what the partner has to do today and cut everything else.
9.challenge: Ask for it once more in twenty seconds and see what survives twice.
9.monitoring: What he CUTS. If the date or the request goes, the hierarchy is not clear yet.
9.evidence: What he cut. It goes in the post-lesson record.
9.transition: Move on when the forty-five seconds have been given.

10.goal: To register what was worked on and to leave the next lesson announced.
10.interaction: S ticks the list; T–S on the close.
run: He ticks what he recognizes. Do not argue with the marks — they are his.
Say that today's recording stays. He asked, in as many words, for a company that could show him how much he had improved. Today is the zero mark, and that is said out loud.
Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class has one optional recording about a real message he got this week, and two podcasts of founders telling the sale of their own company.

Announce lesson 2: listening — ninety seconds of a buyer call, two speakers, and what to do at the point where he loses the thread. It is the one thing he named as the single skill that would fix the others.
exact: This recording stays. In three months we play it again, and you hear the difference yourself — you do not have to take my word for it.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is ticked, read the list with him and ask which line he could use in tomorrow's inbox.
10.challenge: Ask which message in his inbox right now he would answer with what he did today.
10.monitoring: A low mark after two minutes that held is worth recording — it is the gap between doing and knowing that he did.
10.evidence: Fill the post-lesson record BEFORE you close. This is lesson 1 of the four in the block; lesson 4 reads them together.
